The augmented Hessian is diag(1,-1,-1)/3. Compatibility holds, but zero is strictly stable for nominal training and unstable for augmented training. Requiring group invariance of TL would repair this implication. Theorem 3.7 and the augmented-to-equivariant stability implication are unaffected.",

Also, Table 2 and Appendix E.2.1 miscount rotation-invariant circular convolutions: for even N, rotation of convolution offsets has fixed points, giving dimension N²/4 + 2, rather than N²/4; at N=14 this is 51 rather than 49.",

Parameter-distance curves alone do not resolve this distinction.",

strengths: Soundness: The group-averaging identity in Lemma 3.9 and the commuting-projection argument provide a convincing basis for Theorem 3.7. The distinction between parameterization-independent stationary points and parameterization-dependent trajectories is valuable.

Originality: The compatibility condition offers a useful geometric perspective on augmentation versus architectural equivariance, extending the discussion beyond the linear and kernel settings emphasized in the related work.

Significance: Distinguishing equality of stationary-point sets from their transverse stability helps explain why augmentation need not reproduce equivariant training. Appendix A demonstrates the framework's applicability to several architectural families.

Presentation and reproducibility: The definitions, diagrams, and examples make the mathematical framework accessible. A code repository link, 30-run experiments, architectural details, optimizer settings, and computational-resource estimates provide useful reproducibility support.

Limitations and ethics: The manuscript explicitly acknowledges exact Haar averaging, compact-group restrictions, and the unresolved extension to SGD. These are appropriately disclosed limitations. No material research-ethics concern is apparent from the theoretical work and MNIST experiments.
weaknesses: Decisive soundness issue: Theorem 3.11(1) is false under compatibility alone. Its proof assumes positivity of R''(A)[ρ(g)Y,ρ(g)Y], although nominal stability guarantees positivity only on TL, and compatibility does not imply ρ(g)Y belongs to TL. A concrete counterexample uses Z3 fixing e0 and rotating the (e1,e2) plane by 120 degrees, with admissible weights span(e0,e1). For the exponential neuron exp(λ·x), half squared loss, and equally weighted inputs ±e0, ±e1, ±e2 with respective labels 1, 1, 5, zero is stationary and the nominal Hessian is diag(1,1,-3)/3. The augmented Hessian is diag(1,-1,-1)/3. Compatibility holds, but zero is strictly stable for nominal training and unstable for augmented training. Requiring group invariance of TL would repair this implication. Theorem 3.7 and the augmented-to-equivariant stability implication are unaffected.

Further mathematical corrections are needed. Assumptions 1–3 omit regularity conditions needed for differentiating expectations and for the quadratic Taylor remainder in Proposition 3.13. Also, Table 2 and Appendix E.2.1 miscount rotation-invariant circular convolutions: for even N, rotation of convolution offsets has fixed points, giving dimension N²/4 + 2, rather than N²/4; at N=14 this is 51 rather than 49.

Experimental support: Appendix E.2 initializes in E with partially unitary embeddings and full-batch gradient descent, then interprets departures from E as instability. Exact Haar-averaged dynamics preserve E even when it is transversely unstable. The experiments need controlled transverse perturbations, precision checks, and explicit specification of group averaging to establish whether the observed drift reflects instability, sampling effects, or implementation error. Parameter-distance curves alone do not resolve this distinction.

Reproducibility: Appendix E.1 describes LayerNorm only through mean subtraction, omitting variance normalization and possible learned affine parameters. The actual normalization axes and parameter constraints matter for the required equivariance assumption. Likewise, attributing non-unitary outliers to ill-conditioned initialization without quantifying initial projection errors or conditioning leaves an unresolved confound in the parameterization comparison.

Significance is primarily local and structural. The results concern the prescribed layerwise equivariant set E and do not establish attraction toward it from ordinary initialization, convergence benefits, or improved functional equivariance and predictive performance. The MNIST experiments measure parameter drift and therefore provide limited support for the practical recommendations. This restricted reach would be acceptable for a sound theoretical contribution, but it does not offset the incorrect stability theorem.
